name: Amazon
lede: Amazon is a deep forest green; in the jeweller's books the word names Amazon stone, a green feldspar.

sections.title: A stone's name
sections.body:
Finlay's survey of gems lists Amazon stone, a green microcline feldspar, among the green stones, near [[emerald]] and [[jade]] [1]. Finlay also notes that translators of the Bible's list of breastplate stones render two of them, leshem and shoham, as Amazon stone in one reading [1]. Other readings give yellow jasper or green turquoise instead, so the identification is uncertain [1].

The books give no link between this color and the river or the warriors. Pastoureau's green book mentions the Amazons only in passing, in a medieval bestiary where a three-headed dragon comes from their country [2]. That adds nothing to the color's history.

sections.title: The swatch
sections.body: The swatch is a dark, slightly bluish green, darker than [[emerald]] and cooler than [[jade]]. Amazon stone in nature runs from blue-green to a minty green, so this swatch is a name label, not a measurement of the gem. The origin of the color name is undocumented in our books.

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: This green is rare in painting: 38 of 23,781 paintings in our archive hold it, about 0.16 per cent [3]. Its use rises sharply in the 1900s, at 6.4 times the overall rate, and the strongest match is Franz Marc's *Weasels at Play* from 1911, at 36 per cent of the canvas [3][[painting:nga-121096|Weasels at Play]]. Renoir's *A Girl with a Watering Can*, 1876, holds it at 32 per cent [3][[painting:nga-46681|A Girl with a Watering Can]]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so a match is a color on a screen, not a pigment test [3].
